steps.text: Water pieces have a bent shape that fits best in sixes. They join hands to make rings with six sides, like a honeycomb or a tile floor. One ring joins the next ring, and the next.

guess.question: When water pieces lock together, what shape do they love to make?
guess.why: The shape of water pieces fits best in six-sided rings, like a honeycomb.

steps.title: Six corners grow six arms
steps.text: That tiny six-sided seed floats in the cloud. More water sticks to it. The flat sides fill in, but the six corners stick out and catch more water. So six little bumps grow into six arms.

guess.question: A tiny six-sided ice seed starts to grow. How many corners can new pieces stick to?
guess.why: Six sides means six corners, so six bumpy arms start to grow.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: All six arms ride through the same cold, wet air together. So they all grow the same branches at the same time. That is why snowflakes have six matching arms: tiny sixes build a six-sided crystal, and six corners grow into six arms.

steps.title: Make a paper snowflake
steps.text: Try it safe with paper. Fold a circle like a pizza into 6 equal slices. Snip tiny triangles from the folds with help from a grown-up. Open it. You made six matching arms! Real snow does this with ice, not scissors.

steps.title: What if test
steps.text: Let's check your thinking. If the tiny blocks stack in sixes, the big shape must have six parts. That rule never breaks.

guess.question: Imagine pretend water that stacks in sixes, like real water. How many arms would its snowflake have?
guess.why: The small pattern sets the big shape. Sixes below make six arms up top.

steps.title: The man who photographed snow
steps.text: Long ago, a man named Johannes Kepler stared at snow and asked, why always six? Much later, a farmer named Wilson Bentley loved snow so much he took photos of thousands of flakes. His photos showed everyone: always six sides, but every flake a little different!

steps.title: Become a snow detective
steps.text: Next snow day, catch flakes on dark paper and use a magnifier. Can you find a star one? A plate one? A lumpy one? Count the sides. Are they all six?

claims.text: Snow is made of ice crystals formed when water vapor in cold clouds freezes.
Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules that stick to each other.
In ice, water molecules lock into a tidy repeating pattern with six-sided rings.
Because the tiny pattern has six sides, the big ice crystal grows with six sides and can grow six arms.
All six arms of one snowflake grow in the same air at the same time, so they grow in similar ways and look matching.
Johannes Kepler wrote about six-sided snow in 1611 and Wilson Bentley photographed thousands of snowflakes in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
claims.uncertainty: Exact dates and counts vary by source; the six-sided observation is well supported.

claims.text: Many snow crystals are simple lumps or plates, not perfect star shapes; star shapes need just-right cold and damp air.

sources.title: National Snow and Ice Data Center - All About Snow

output.title: Is the nautilus a golden spiral?
output.summary: The nautilus shell is a growing spiral, but not a golden spiral because it widens too slowly.
learningObjectives: Tell the difference between any logarithmic spiral and the special golden spiral
Explain why a nautilus shell looks like a golden spiral but grows at the wrong rate to be one
misconceptionNotes: Many books and pictures label a nautilus shell as a golden-ratio spiral; measurements show the match is only rough, not exact.

steps.title: A perfect-looking coil
steps.text: You see a flat, striped coil with many chambers, small in the middle and getting bigger toward the opening. It looks very neat and even, so people often ask: did nature draw a perfect golden-ratio pattern here?

steps.title: Short answer: close, but no
steps.text: No. The nautilus shell is close to a widening spiral, but it is not a golden-ratio spiral. It widens too slowly to match the golden ratio.

steps.title: Growing without changing shape
steps.text: Basic truth 1: some shapes grow by multiplying. Think of blowing up a photo: every part gets, say, 1.2 times bigger. A logarithmic spiral works like that: each turn is a multiplied copy of the last, so the shape stays the same while the size grows.

guess.question: If a spiral keeps exactly the same shape while getting bigger, does it grow by adding or by multiplying?
options: Add the same amount each turn, like 1 cm wider
Multiply by the same amount each turn, like 1.2 times wider
guess.why: Adding the same width would change the shape. Multiplying by the same factor each turn keeps the proportions and makes a logarithmic spiral.

steps.title: What golden would require
steps.text: Basic truth 2: golden spiral is a strict recipe. The golden ratio is a number, about 1.618. A golden spiral must get about 1.618 times farther from the center every quarter-turn. Any other steady rate is a different spiral.

guess.question: What makes a golden spiral special?
options: One exact growth rate: about 1.618 times wider every quarter-turn
Any steady growth rate that looks smooth
guess.why: Many spirals multiply steadily, but only one uses the golden ratio, about 1.618, every quarter-turn. That exact rate is what golden means here.

steps.title: Room by room
steps.text: The animal lives in the outer chamber. As it grows, it builds a new, slightly larger chamber at the opening. The old chambers stay behind. Repeating bigger-but-similar rooms naturally makes a coiled, widening shell.

guess.question: How does a nautilus make its shell bigger?
options: It remakes its whole shell at once
It adds one bigger room at the open end
guess.why: The animal lives in the last chamber and builds a new, slightly larger chamber in front as it grows, leaving the old ones empty for float.

steps.title: Measure the widening
steps.text: When people measure real shells, the coil widens by roughly 1.1 to 1.3 times per quarter-turn, not 1.618 times. Numbers differ a little by animal and photo, but they are clearly below golden growth.

guess.question: Photos show the nautilus is only about 1.1 to 1.3 times wider each quarter-turn. Compared with 1.618, what does that mean?
options: Much less than 1.618, so it grows more tightly
Much more than 1.618, so it grows more openly
guess.why: 1.1 to 1.3 is smaller than 1.618, so the real shell hugs the center more tightly than a true golden spiral would.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the nautilus follows the general rule, steady multiplying growth, so it looks like a logarithmic spiral. But it fails the strict golden test because its multiplier is too small. It is a spiral, not the golden spiral.

guess.question: A shell can be a logarithmic spiral but still fail to be golden. Why?
options: Yes, because every smooth coil is golden
No, because golden needs one exact growth rate
guess.why: Logarithmic only means steady multiplying growth. Golden means that multiplier must be 1.618 per quarter-turn, which the nautilus does not have.

steps.title: Check it on paper
steps.text: Safe test: print a photo of a nautilus. Mark the center. Measure the width of the coil with a ruler at four points, each a quarter-turn around. Divide each width by the one before it. You should get numbers near 1.1 to 1.3, not 1.6. If you draw a true golden spiral on clear plastic, laying it over the shell also shows the golden one opens out too fast.

steps.title: What if it were golden?
steps.text: Use the rule in a new case: imagine the nautilus suddenly switched to true golden growth. After one full turn, four multiplications by 1.618 would make it about 6.85 times wider. The real shell grows far less than that, so a true golden shell would look puffed open by comparison.

guess.question: Suppose a shell really did grow 1.618 times wider every quarter-turn. Would it look like your nautilus?
options: No, because it would open outward much faster
Yes, it would look exactly the same
guess.why: After a few turns, multiplying by 1.618 each quarter-turn makes the shell much larger and more open than the tight nautilus coil.

steps.title: Who figured out the spiral
steps.text: In the 1600s Jakob Bernoulli studied this kind of multiply-to-grow curve and called it the logarithmic spiral. He was struck that it stays the same shape as it grows. Later writers loved the beauty of shells and sometimes guessed they must use the famous golden ratio, but careful measurement showed the nautilus has its own slower rate.

steps.title: Where golden really shows up
steps.text: Look next at a sunflower head or pinecone. People also call those golden, and there the math fits much better. Ask: what is the growth rate, and can I measure it? That habit, measure the multiplier, lets you rebuild the answer anywhere.

claims.text: A logarithmic spiral is a curve that keeps the same shape while growing larger by multiplying its distance from the center with each turn.
A golden spiral is one specific logarithmic spiral that gets wider by the golden ratio, about 1.618, every quarter-turn.
A chambered nautilus grows by adding larger chambers one after another at the opening, so the whole shell gets bigger while keeping about the same coiled shape.
Measured nautilus shells grow more slowly than a golden spiral does, with a width increase per quarter-turn closer to about 1.1 to 1.3 rather than 1.618.
claims.uncertainty: Exact numbers vary between animals and studies and how the photo is measured; the key point is it is clearly less than 1.618.

claims.text: A nautilus shell is close to a logarithmic spiral in overall shape, but it is not a golden spiral because its growth rate does not match the golden ratio.
The mathematician Jakob Bernoulli studied the logarithmic spiral in the 1600s and found it keeps the same shape as it grows.

output.title: How a leaf cooks with sunshine
output.summary: A leaf uses green chlorophyll to catch light energy and turn water and air into sugar food, letting out oxygen.
learningObjectives: Say in own words that a leaf uses light energy to turn air and water into sugar food
Name chlorophyll as the green catcher of sunlight
misconceptionNotes: Sunlight alone is not the food. Sunlight gives the energy to join water and carbon dioxide into sugar food.

steps.title: A green leaf in the sun
steps.text: You see a flat, thin, green leaf sitting in bright sun. It does not move, eat, or chew. So here is the puzzle: how can a still leaf make food from sunshine?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: The leaf catches sunlight with its green color. It uses the light power to turn air and water into sugar food.

steps.title: Living things need food energy
steps.text: You need food to run and grow. A plant needs food too. Food is stored energy the body can use.

guess.question: Like you, a growing plant needs what?
options: It needs food energy to grow
guess.why: All living things need food energy to grow and live.

steps.title: Sunlight brings energy
steps.text: Sunshine is not just bright. It carries energy. You can feel it warm your skin. That energy can do work and make changes.

guess.question: Stand in sun and then in shade. Does sunlight bring energy?
options: Yes, light brings energy you can feel
guess.why: You feel warmer and see brighter in sun, so sunlight carries energy.

steps.title: The green catcher
steps.text: The leaf is wide and flat to catch lots of sun. Inside is green stuff called chlorophyll. Say: KLOR-oh-fill. It grabs light energy like a solar panel.

guess.question: What catches the sunlight in the leaf?
guess.why: The leaf is green because chlorophyll is inside, and chlorophyll catches light.

steps.title: Water and air come in
steps.text: A plant drinks water with its roots. The water travels up to the leaf. The leaf also breathes in air through tiny holes under it. The air has a gas called carbon dioxide.

guess.question: Besides light, what else must the leaf bring in to cook?
guess.why: The recipe needs water from roots and carbon dioxide gas from air.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: chlorophyll holds the light energy. That power joins water and carbon dioxide into sweet sugar. Sugar is the plant food. Leftover oxygen floats out into the air we breathe.

guess.question: With light power, air plus water change into what?
guess.why: Light powers the mix to become sugar the plant eats, and oxygen goes out.

steps.title: Feel sun and spot green
steps.text: Try this safe look: with a grown-up, feel a leaf in bright sun and one in deep shade. Which feels warmer? Or look closely at a leaf to spot the green and the lines that carry water. Green plus light plus water is the cooking team.

steps.title: What about night?
steps.text: Think of a kitchen with no power. At night, with no sunlight power, the leaf cannot cook new sugar. In the day, cooking starts again.

guess.question: Night comes. No sun. What does the leaf kitchen do?
options: It stops making food until light comes back
guess.why: No light energy means no power to run the air-plus-water recipe.

steps.title: Who saw it first?
steps.text: Long ago, a man named Jan Ingenhousz watched plants in light and dark. He found plants in light changed the air in a good way. That helped people find the leaf food recipe.

steps.title: Food for the whole world
steps.text: Leaf food feeds more than the plant. Bugs, birds, and you eat plants or animals that ate plants. And the oxygen leaves let out is the air we breathe. Watch for leaves turning to face the sun.

claims.text: Living plants need food energy to grow and stay alive, and they make sugar as food.
Sunlight carries energy that can be felt as light and warmth and can power changes.
Leaves look green because they contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that catches light energy.
Leaves take in carbon dioxide gas from air through tiny holes and water carried up from roots.
In photosynthesis light energy powers a change that turns carbon dioxide and water into sugar glucose and releases oxygen.
Plants use the sugar for energy and growth, and the released oxygen goes into the air.
In the 1770s Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants in light change the air, which helped reveal photosynthesis.

output.title: Where does wood really come from?
output.summary: A tree's wood is not eaten soil. Leaves take carbon dioxide from air and use sunlight to join it with water into sugar, then link sugars into wood.
learningObjectives: Explain why most of a tree's wood comes from air and water, not soil
Trace atoms from carbon dioxide and water through photosynthesis into wood
misconceptionNotes: It feels like trees eat soil like we eat food, but soil mainly gives water and small amounts of minerals, not the bulk for wood.

steps.title: A huge tree from a little soil
steps.text: Look at a leaf, then at the trunk. That trunk can weigh tons. The soil around the tree does not have a giant hole in it. So where did all that heavy wood come from? It looks like it should have come from the soil, but the soil is still there.

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: No. Almost all of a tree's wood comes from air and water. The leaf pulls carbon dioxide from the air, the roots pull water, and the tree links them together to build wood.

steps.title: Nothing grows from nothing
steps.text: First truth: stuff is made of atoms, and you cannot make atoms from nothing. To get bigger, the tree must grab atoms from somewhere. The only choices are air, water, and soil.

guess.question: A tree trunk gets heavier each year. What must be true?
options: It was created from pure energy with no atoms needed.
It must have taken atoms in from air, water, or soil.
guess.why: Matter is not made from nothing. Extra wood means extra atoms came from outside the tree.

steps.title: Invisible building parts
steps.text: Second truth: air is not empty. It holds carbon dioxide: one carbon plus two oxygens. Water is H2O: hydrogen plus oxygen. Jargon check: carbon dioxide is just a tiny gas piece of air that plants use as food building blocks.

guess.question: Wood is full of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Could air and water supply them?
options: Air has a gas with carbon in it, and soil water has hydrogen and oxygen.
Air and water have no carbon, hydrogen, or oxygen to give.
guess.why: Air contains carbon dioxide, which has carbon and oxygen. Water is H2O, hydrogen and oxygen. So yes.

steps.title: The leaf kitchen
steps.text: The leaf is a kitchen. Tiny holes underneath let carbon dioxide in. Veins bring water from the roots. Green dye called chlorophyll catches sunlight for energy. With that energy the leaf rebuilds carbon dioxide and water into sugar and lets oxygen go out.

guess.question: A leaf takes in carbon dioxide + water + light energy. What comes out?
guess.why: The leaf's green dye, chlorophyll, catches light energy and uses it to remake those atoms into sugar. Leftover oxygen leaves through tiny leaf holes.

steps.title: From sugar to wood
steps.text: Sugar is the brick. The tree links thousands of sugar bricks into long fibers called cellulose, then glues them with a stiff material called lignin. That is wood and bark. The carbon in those chains came straight from the air.

guess.question: Sugar is soft and dissolves. Wood is hard and lasts for years. What must the tree do to the sugar?
options: Burn the sugar right away for heat only.
Link sugars into long, strong chains.
guess.why: Wood is mostly cellulose: thousands of sugars linked into fibers, plus glue-like lignin. Linking makes it strong.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the soil gives water plus tiny minerals, but the bulk, the carbon skeleton of wood, comes from carbon dioxide in the air. So a giant tree is mostly solid air + water, built with sunlight energy in its leaves.

steps.title: See leaves breathe
steps.text: Try this safe test: find a green houseplant in sunlight. Slip a clear plastic bag gently over one leaf and tie loosely for a few hours in the day. You will see tiny water drops inside. That is water moving out of leaf holes, proof leaves trade gases and water with air. Do not leave it on for days or in hot sun.

steps.title: The potted-tree test
steps.text: Now use the idea. Imagine your tree in a pot on a scale. If wood came from soil, the soil would vanish as the tree grew. In real life the tree gets heavy while the soil stays almost the same.

guess.question: If you grew a 100-pound tree in a pot and weighed the soil before and after, what would you see?
options: It would barely shrink, because the tree is mostly not from soil.
It would leave a huge pit, because the tree ate the soil.
guess.why: Soil loses only water and a few minerals. The carbon weight is new from the air, so soil weight barely changes.

steps.title: The willow that weighed the air
steps.text: About 400 years ago Jan Baptista van Helmont did that exact test. He grew a willow tree for 5 years, watering it only. The tree gained over 160 pounds, but the soil lost less than a few ounces. He proved wood does not come mostly from soil.

steps.title: Trees are solid sky
steps.text: Go further: this means forests pull carbon from the sky and lock it into wood. When wood burns or rots, that carbon goes back to the air. That loop is a big part of climate and why planting trees matters, but does not undo fossil fuels by itself.

claims.text: Matter is not created from nothing; to grow, a plant must get atoms from somewhere else.
Air contains carbon dioxide, a gas made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Roots take up water from the soil, which provides hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
Leaves use energy from sunlight captured by chlorophyll to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen.
Wood is mostly long chains of sugar called cellulose and lignin that the tree builds from simple sugars.
Most of the dry weight of a tree comes from carbon dioxide from the air, not from soil.
In the 1600s Jan Baptista van Helmont grew a willow for 5 years and found the tree gained much weight while the soil lost only a tiny amount.

output.title: How bees find home
output.summary: Bees fly home using the sun to keep direction, then eyes and nose to find their hive spot.
learningObjectives: Bees use the sun to keep direction.
Bees remember what the hive area looks and smells like.
Bees put clues together to get home.
misconceptionNotes: Bees do not use maps or GPS like people. They use the sun, what their eyes see, and what their nose smells.

steps.title: A tiny flyer in a big world
steps.text: You see a little honey bee buzz, buzz, buzz from flower to flower. Then whoosh! She flies away and finds her tiny hive again. The sky is big. All the flowers look the same. How does she not get lost?

steps.title: The quick answer
steps.text: She uses the sun to stay on track, then looks and sniffs for her home place. It is like following a big light, then finding your street, then your front door.

steps.title: The sun is a pointer
steps.text: First truth: the sun is a bright, steady pointer. It is in the east in the morning and west at night. If you keep the sun on the same side of you, you walk in a straight line.

guess.question: On a short trip, does the sun give a steady direction to follow?
options: Yes, the sun stays in about the same line to guide them
No, the sun jumps all around every minute
guess.why: The sun moves slowly, so for a short bee trip it is a steady pointer.

steps.title: Eyes see, noses smell
steps.text: Second truth: animals remember with eyes and nose. Eyes notice big shapes like trees and houses. Noses notice smells like flowers and honey. Your brain saves them like pictures.

guess.question: How do animals learn a place?
guess.why: Eyes see shapes and colors. Noses smell smells. Brains remember them.

steps.title: Sun on one side
steps.text: The bee has big eyes that see the sun and sky light. She picks: keep the sun on my left. Now she can fly straight and not go in circles.

guess.question: A bee wants to fly straight home. What helps?
options: Keep the sun on the same side to fly straight
Fly in circles to be silly
guess.why: Keeping the sun on one side helps hold a straight line.

steps.title: Look and sniff near home
steps.text: Close to home, the bee looks for clues. That tree! That bush! That color box! Her hive and sisters have a special home smell. Eyes and nose say: this is it!

guess.question: Which is easier for a bee to find again?
options: A plain white wall with no smell
A big red tree and sweet hive smell
guess.why: A special look and smell is easier to remember.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the bee flies far with the sun as her compass. Then she uses remembered shapes and home smells to land at the right hive. Far pointer, then near clues. Home!

guess.question: How does the bee get all the way home?
options: Sun for far, eyes and nose for near
guess.why: Far clues plus near clues lead her step by step to the hive.

steps.title: Be a bee
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up outside. Pick a tree far away. Walk to it while keeping the sun on the same shoulder. Now turn and walk back keeping the sun on the other shoulder. What landmarks did you remember?

steps.title: A cloudy day
steps.text: Think: bees love sunny days. On a very cloudy, windy day, some clues are gone. Can she still get home with landmarks?

guess.question: If clouds hid the sun all day and wind blew smells away, what would happen?
options: It would be harder to know which way to go
guess.why: With sun and smell clues gone, the bee must rely only on what she sees.

steps.title: The bee watcher
steps.text: Long ago, a man named Karl von Frisch watched bees very closely. He found they even dance to tell friends where flowers are! He won a big prize, the Nobel Prize, for learning how animals talk and find their way.

steps.title: Watch like a scientist
steps.text: Next time you see a bee, stay still and safe. Watch which way she flies. Is the sun out? What flowers or trees could be her landmarks?

claims.text: Honey bees live together in a colony in a hive and fly out to find nectar and pollen, then return.
Bees can use the position of the sun in the sky as a compass to keep their direction.
Bees also learn landmarks, shapes, and smells around the hive to find the exact home spot.
claims.uncertainty: Exact mix of landmarks and smell varies by study; simplified for a child.

claims.text: Bees have large compound eyes for seeing light patterns and a strong sense of smell.
Karl von Frisch studied honey bee dances that tell other bees where to go, and won the Nobel Prize in 1973 for work on animal behavior.

sources.title: Nobel Prize - Karl von Frisch facts

output.title: Why bananas brown faster next to other fruit
output.summary: Ripe fruits release ethylene gas that drifts through air; bananas sense it and ripen faster, reaching soft brown spots sooner.
learningObjectives: Explain that ripening fruits release ethylene gas into the air
Explain how extra ethylene from neighbors speeds up banana ripening and browning
Predict how separating fruit or trapping air changes ripening speed
misconceptionNotes: Brown spots do not always mean the banana is rotten or unsafe - they usually mean it is very ripe and sweeter; look and smell for sour, mold, or oozing as signs of spoilage.

steps.title: Yellow alone, brown in a crowd
steps.text: A banana alone on the counter stays yellow for days. Put that same banana in a bowl touching apples or avocados, and in a day or two it is speckled brown and soft. The puzzle: the banana did not change, so what is coming from the other fruit that speeds it up?

steps.title: The short answer
steps.text: Other ripe fruits release a ripening gas called ethylene. Your banana senses it in the air and ripens faster, so it turns brown sooner.

steps.title: Air carries invisible messages
steps.text: Truth 1: gases spread through air. Ethylene is a simple gas made by plants. You cannot see or smell it at these tiny amounts, but it floats from fruit into the surrounding air. Jargon check: a hormone is just a chemical message that tells a living thing to do something.

guess.question: Ethylene is a gas at room temperature. How do you think it can get from an apple to a nearby banana?
guess.why: Gases spread and mix in air, so molecules released by one fruit can reach the skin of a neighbor.

steps.title: Picked fruit still listens
steps.text: Truth 2: picked fruit is still alive and can respond. A banana is living tissue with stored energy in starch. It can sense chemical signals and switch on ripening work: make sugars, soften walls, and lose green color.

guess.question: A picked banana still turns from green to yellow to brown. Which is it more like?
options: A living thing that can change after picking
A dead object like a stone
guess.why: Picked fruit is still living tissue. Its cells can sense signals and run ripening changes using stored starch and energy.

steps.title: A shared cloud of gas
steps.text: Fruits share one bowl of air. Bananas make their own ethylene, and neighbors like apples, pears, avocados, and tomatoes add more. Next to other fruit, the banana sits in a stronger cloud of ethylene than it would alone.

guess.question: Apples, pears, and avocados also release ethylene. What does a banana piled next to them experience?
options: More ethylene in the air around them
guess.why: Each fruit adds its own ethylene to the shared bowl of air, so the level around the banana rises.

steps.title: The switch gets turned up
steps.text: Ethylene flips the ripening switch. When the banana skin senses the gas, its cells speed up the ripening jobs: starch becomes sugar, the flesh softens, green color fades. A ripening banana then makes even more ethylene itself.

guess.question: Ethylene tells fruit tissue to ripen. If a banana senses extra ethylene, what happens next?
options: Ripen faster and make even more ethylene
guess.why: Ripening bananas respond by ripening faster and producing more ethylene themselves, which is why ripening can speed up once it starts.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: neighbor fruit raises ethylene in the air. The banana senses it, ripens faster, and makes more ethylene too. It rushes through yellow to soft and speckled brown sooner than it would alone.

guess.question: If all ripening steps run faster, what happens to the timing of brown spots?
options: It reaches very ripe and brown sooner
guess.why: Brown speckles are a late stage after much ripening work and softening, so faster ripening means earlier browning.

steps.title: Bag vs. alone
steps.text: Safe test: take two similar green-yellow bananas. Keep one alone on one counter. Put the other in a loose paper bag with a ripe apple, folded shut but not airtight. Check color and firmness daily for 3 days. The bag traps ethylene, so the bagged banana should yellow and spot first. Do not use a sealed plastic bag for long storage, and wash hands and fruit before eating.

steps.title: Who else talks through air?
steps.text: Use the same idea elsewhere. Grocers often say to keep onions away from potatoes because gases and moisture from onions make potatoes sprout faster. Different gas, same logic: shared air carries a message that changes the neighbor.

guess.question: Where else might one food's gas change its neighbor?
options: Bread going stale next to crackers
guess.why: Onions also release gases and moisture that can push potatoes to sprout, just as ethylene from one fruit pushes another to ripen.

steps.title: The leaky lamp clue
steps.text: In 1901, Russian student Dimitry Neljubow noticed that pea seedlings bent strangely near leaky gas lamps. He showed the cause was tiny amounts of ethylene in the lighting gas. Later scientists proved plants make ethylene themselves, and that it controls ripening — the reason we now ripen bananas with care and keep some fruits apart.

steps.title: Control the cloud
steps.text: Want slower browning? Give bananas space, airflow, and distance from high-ethylene fruits. Want faster ripening? Do the opposite: group green bananas or avocados with a ripe apple in paper. What would you change if you wanted bananas ready exactly on Saturday?

claims.text: Ethylene is a simple gas that acts as a plant hormone controlling ripening and other growth responses.
Bananas naturally make ethylene, and make more of it as they ripen.
Many common fruits, such as apples, pears, avocados, and tomatoes, also release ethylene as they ripen.
During ripening, starches turn to sugars, green color is lost, flesh softens, and banana skin later develops brown spots.
Brown spots on very ripe bananas come from later breakdown of skin cells and browning reactions after ripening is far along.
claims.uncertainty: Exact browning chemistry varies by variety and damage; described here in simplified form for a plain-level lesson.

claims.text: In 1901 Russian scientist Dimitry Neljubow showed that ethylene gas from lighting gas altered plant growth, leading to later work on ethylene as a plant hormone.
Ethylene moves through air, so ethylene made by one fruit can reach and affect nearby fruit.

problems.question: A picked banana still turns from green to yellow to brown. Which is it more like?
problems.problem: The marked answer is incorrect; a picked banana is more like a living thing that can change after picking.

output.title: How a cactus lives without much water
output.summary: A cactus lives with little water by drinking rain fast, storing it in a fat stem, and losing very little through spines and waxy skin.
learningObjectives: Tell that plants need water but also lose water to air.
Name 3 cactus parts that save water: fat stem, spines, waxy skin.
Explain that a cactus saves water, stores water, and grabs rain fast.
misconceptionNotes: A cactus does need some water - it does not live on zero water, it is just very good at saving and storing it.
Spines do not suck up water like straws; they mostly save water and protect the water inside.

steps.title: A fat plant in a dry place
steps.text: Look at this green, fat, spiky plant. It lives in hot, dry sand where it may not rain for months. Leaves on most plants are big and soft. So why does this plant have no big leaves, only spikes, and why is it so fat? How can it stay alive without much water?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: A cactus stays alive by saving water, storing water, and drinking fast. Its fat stem holds water, its spines and waxy skin let very little water escape.

steps.title: Plants need water
steps.text: First truth: all green plants need water. Plants mix water with air and light to make their food. No water at all means no life. So a cactus cannot live on zero water.

guess.question: Does a cactus need water at all?
options: It needs some water to live and make food
guess.why: All green plants need some water to make food, so a cactus needs water too. It just uses very little.

steps.title: Water escapes to air
steps.text: Second truth: water escapes into dry air. A wet towel dries. Puddles shrink. Plants leak water the same way from their leaves. Hot, dry, windy air pulls water out faster. Jargon: this leak is called transpiration.

guess.question: What happens to water on a hot, dry, windy day?
options: Water leaves into the air, like steam from soup
guess.why: Water escapes into dry air as tiny invisible vapor. That is why wet things dry out.

steps.title: Fat stem stores water
steps.text: The stem is a water bottle. The fat green middle is full of soft, wet tissue that holds water for months. Round and fat means lots of water inside, with less skin to leak from.

guess.question: If you must save water for months, which shape helps more?
guess.why: A fat, round shape holds a lot inside but has less skin for water to escape from.

steps.title: Spines instead of leaves
steps.text: Spines are tiny leaves. Big soft leaves are great for catching light, but they leak lots of water. A cactus traded big leaves for sharp spines. Spines leak almost no water, give a little shade, and poke animals that want a drink.

guess.question: Which loses less water in the desert?
guess.why: Big flat leaves have lots of surface for water to escape. Small spikes have almost none.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: when rain comes, wide shallow roots drink very fast and fill the fat stem. Then waxy skin seals the water in, like cling wrap on food. Tiny breathing holes open mostly at cool night, so the plant gets air without losing much water. Save, store, drink fast - that is how it lives without much water.

steps.title: Wrap keeps water in
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: put two same wet paper towels out. Cover one loosely with clear wrap. Leave the other open. Check every hour. Which stays wet longer? That is what waxy skin does for a cactus.

steps.title: Design a dry-place plant
steps.text: Think: if you moved a cactus to a wet jungle, would its tricks still help? And what would help a jungle plant most?

guess.question: You build a plant for a very dry roof garden. What do you pick?
options: Big leaves and thin stem, to catch more sun
Fat stem, waxy skin, and spines, to save water
guess.why: Use the cactus trick: store water inside and let little escape.

steps.title: People meet the cactus
steps.text: Long ago, people in the dry Americas learned which cacti held safe water and fruit. When visitors from Europe arrived in the 1500s, they had never seen such spiky water-bottles. They wrote about them, drew them, and carried some home. Later plant scientists compared them and saw spines are just changed leaves.

steps.title: Find other water savers
steps.text: Look next: cut an apple and a grape. Which dries out faster? Find other water-savers like aloe. Ask: where else do animals or people store water for dry times?

claims.text: Green plants use water plus air and light to make food in photosynthesis.
Plants lose water as vapor from leaves into air, called transpiration, and lose more when it is hot, dry, or windy.
Cacti are plants that grow naturally mostly in dry places in North and South America.
Many cacti have thick, fleshy stems that can store a lot of water inside, like a water bottle.
Cactus spines are sharp, changed leaves that lose very little water and help shade the plant and keep thirsty animals away.
Cacti have waxy skin and tiny holes that open mostly at cool night time to take in air while losing less water.
claims.uncertainty: Exact night-opening behavior varies by kind of cactus, but waxy coat and water-saving holes are widely described for cacti.

claims.text: Many cacti have wide, shallow roots near the surface that can quickly soak up rain when it falls.
claims.uncertainty: Root shape varies by species; wide shallow roots are common in desert cacti but not in all.

claims.text: People in the Americas used cacti for food and water for a very long time, and European visitors in the 1500s first wrote about and named these strange spiny plants.
claims.uncertainty: Early dates vary by source; general story of long Indigenous use and 1500s European description is supported.

output.title: Why veins look blue
output.summary: Blood is always red. Veins look blue because skin scatters blue light back while dark venous blood absorbs red light.
learningObjectives: Explain that venous blood is dark red, not blue
Use light absorption and scattering to explain why veins look blue through skin
misconceptionNotes: Blood is not blue inside veins; textbook diagrams color veins blue only as a label, not as the real color.

steps.title: Blue lines, red blood
steps.text: Look at the inside of your wrist. You see thin blue-green lines under pale skin. If you cut yourself or give blood, though, the blood that comes out is red. So why does it look blue when it is inside?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Your blood is never blue. It is always red. Veins only look blue because of how light goes through skin and is soaked up by dark red blood.

steps.title: Color is light bouncing back
steps.text: First truth: color comes from light. White daylight is a mix of rainbow colors. An object looks red if it soaks up other colors and sends red back to your eyes. Jargon: hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that grabs oxygen. It has iron in it, and like rust, it looks red.

guess.question: If you put a drop of blood from a vein on white paper, what color will it be?
options: Red, because of hemoglobin with iron
guess.why: Hemoglobin with iron makes all blood red. Vein blood is dark red because it has given up much oxygen, but it has no blue pigment.

steps.title: Skin is like fog
steps.text: Second truth: skin is not a clear window. Think of skin and the fat under it like fog. Light going in gets bounced around and partly soaked up. That filtering changes what comes back out to your eyes.

guess.question: What does skin do to light?
options: It passes straight through like glass
It soaks up some colors and bounces other colors around
guess.why: Skin is not clear glass. It absorbs some light and scatters, or bounces around, the rest.

steps.title: What is in the tube
steps.text: Your wrist veins carry blood back toward the heart after it dropped off oxygen. Hemoglobin changes from bright cherry-red when full of oxygen to darker brick-red when low. Still red, just darker.

guess.question: Blood in a wrist vein compared to blood in an artery is:
options: Darker red, because it already dropped off oxygen
Bright blue, because veins add blue color
guess.why: Both are red. Vein blood is darker red after delivering oxygen to the body.

steps.title: Red gets trapped, blue escapes
steps.text: Now add light. Red light dives deeper into skin and hits the vein, where dark red blood soaks it up. Blue light cannot dive as deep. It bounces around in the skin above and around the vein and comes back to your eyes.

guess.question: If dark blood soaks up red light strongly, what light is left to reach your eye?
options: Blue is soaked up and red is sent back
Red is soaked up and blue is sent back
guess.why: When red is removed by absorption, the leftover light that scatters back looks blue-green.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: dark red blood + skin on top = blue look. The vein removes red light. Your eye gets back mostly blue-green light from the skin. Your brain says blue vein, even though the tube underneath is full of dark red blood.

guess.question: Why does a red tube under skin look different than a red tube on top of skin?
options: Bright red, because you see true color
guess.why: Under skin you only see the leftover light after red is absorbed, so your brain reads it as blue.

steps.title: Push the blood away
steps.text: Safe test: press a clear drinking glass gently on a blue-looking vein. Pressing pushes blood away for a second. The blue fades and skin looks pale. Let go and dark blood refills the tube and the blue comes back. You did not change blood color, you changed how much red-absorbing blood was under the skin.

steps.title: Where is the filter thinner?
steps.text: Think: bruises, lips, or the inside of your cheek look red-purple because blood is very close to the surface with less pale skin on top. Deeper veins in darker or thicker skin are harder to see. If the blue were real pigment, covering or removing skin would not change it.

guess.question: If you could look at that same vein with the skin peeled back safely, like a surgeon does, what would you see?
options: Redder and darker, because there is less skin filtering
guess.why: Without skin scattering light and trapping red, you would see the true dark red of venous blood.

steps.title: Everyone saw red
steps.text: People long thought veins carried blue blood. When doctors in the 1600s traced how blood loops around, starting with William Harvey in 1628, and later when blood draws became common, everyone could see it: blood from a vein is dark red the moment it leaves the body. The blue was a trick of viewing through skin, and blue in diagrams is just a label.

steps.title: Blue without blue paint
steps.text: The same trick shows up elsewhere. Deep water looks blue even though a glass of water is clear, and blue eyes have no blue pigment, just light scattering. Next time you see a map with red arteries and blue veins, remember: it is a code, not a photo.

claims.text: Human blood is always red inside the body; blood in veins is a dark red, not blue.
Hemoglobin, the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, makes blood look red.
White daylight is a mix of colors of light, including red and blue, which interact differently with skin and blood.
Red light goes deeper into skin and is strongly absorbed by dark venous blood, while blue light does not go as deep and is more scattered and reflected back to the eye.
Wrist veins sit just under thin, light-colored skin and fat, so light filtering through skin affects their color.
William Harvey described blood circulating in a loop in 1628, and surgeons and blood draws since then show venous blood on leaving the body is dark red.

output.title: Why does iron go orange and flaky?
output.summary: Iron meets oxygen and water in air and makes rust, a new orange, soft, flaky stuff that falls off and lets more rust form.
learningObjectives: Say that rust is new stuff made when iron, water, and oxygen meet.
Explain that rust is orange and flaky because it is weak and crumbly, not like strong iron.
misconceptionNotes: Rust is not paint or dirt sitting on iron, and iron is not just changing color - rust is a new crumbly stuff made from the iron itself.

steps.title: A grey nail turns orange
steps.text: You see a nail. It was once grey, smooth, and hard. Now it has bumpy orange spots. Little bits fall off when you touch it. Why did strong grey iron turn into soft orange flakes?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Iron turns orange and flaky because it joins with water and oxygen in the air. Together they make rust, a new orange, soft, crumbly stuff.

steps.title: Iron starts strong
steps.text: First truth: iron is a building stuff. New iron is grey, hard, and strong. You can make nails and bridges from it.

guess.question: New iron is grey and smooth. Is it hard and strong?
guess.why: Yes. Iron starts hard and strong, so the soft flakes must be something new.

steps.title: Air and water touch everything
steps.text: Second truth: air is not empty. Air has a gas called oxygen. Damp air and rain also bring water. Oxygen and water can touch all sides of a nail.

guess.question: Air looks empty, but what is really in damp air?
options: oxygen we breathe and tiny water drops
guess.why: Air holds oxygen and tiny water bits. Both can touch the nail.

steps.title: Three things make a new thing
steps.text: When iron, water, and oxygen stay touching, they stick together. They do not just sit there. They make a whole new stuff called rust.

guess.question: When iron, oxygen, and water stay together, what do they do?
options: stick together and make new stuff
guess.why: They stick together to make rust, called iron oxide.

steps.title: Rust is different
steps.text: Rust does not look or feel like iron. Iron is grey and hard. Rust is orange-brown. Rust is soft and crumbly, like dry cookie crumbs.

guess.question: Iron is grey and hard. Rust is what?
guess.why: Rust is orange and soft. It looks and feels different because it is different.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: rust is puffy and weak, so it cracks and falls off. That shows fresh iron below. The fresh iron meets water and oxygen again and makes more rust. That is why the nail goes orange and flaky and gets thinner.

guess.question: Rust is soft and puffy. What happens when you poke it?
guess.why: It cracks and falls off. That opens a hole so more iron can meet air and water and make more rust.

steps.title: Wet or dry nail?
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Take two clean iron nails. Put one in a dry closed jar. Put one in a jar with a little water, open to air. Look each day for a week. Which one gets more orange spots? The wet one should, because rust needs both water and air.

steps.title: Bikes in rain
steps.text: Think: you leave one bike out in the rain and keep one dry inside. What will happen? Use what you learned about water, air, and rust.

guess.question: Two bikes: one kept dry inside, one left in rain. Which gets orange flakes?
options: the wet bike gets orange flakes
guess.why: The wet bike gets more rust because it gets more water plus air.

steps.title: Finding the hidden gas
steps.text: Long ago, everyone saw iron rust, but no one knew why. In the 1770s, Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele found that air has a gas called oxygen. Later people showed oxygen plus water turns iron into rust.

steps.title: Stop the orange?
steps.text: Next time, look: can you keep rust away? Paint, oil, or dry boxes keep water and air off iron. Why would that help? What orange spots can you find on gates, cars, or tools?

claims.text: Iron is a grey, hard, strong metal element.
Air contains oxygen gas and often tiny bits of water as dampness or rain.
Rust forms when iron touches both oxygen and water at the same time, making a new stuff called iron oxide.
Rust is orange-brown in color.
Rust is soft, crumbly, and flaky, not strong like iron, and it flakes off so fresh iron below can keep rusting.
In the 1770s, scientists Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele showed oxygen is a separate gas in air.

output.title: What burns in a candle?
output.summary: Candle wax is the fuel. Heat melts it, the wick pulls it up, heat turns it to vapor, and that vapor burns with oxygen.
learningObjectives: Explain that wax vapor is the main fuel in a candle flame
Describe how the wick uses capillary action to deliver melted wax to the flame
Use fuel + oxygen + heat to reason about why a candle behaves as it does
misconceptionNotes: It is easy to think the wick is what burns like a tiny campfire log. The wick does char a little, but it is mostly a delivery tube — the wax is the fuel that gets used up.

steps.title: A flame that eats wax
steps.text: You light a candle. The wick glows, a flame stands up, and over hours the wax around it disappears and leaves a hollow. The wick gets black on top but is still there. So here is the puzzle: if the flame sits on the wick, why does the wax vanish?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: The wax is what actually burns. The wick is just the starter and holder — it soaks up melted wax and keeps the flame in place so hot wax vapor can burn.

steps.title: Fire needs three things
steps.text: First truth: fire is not a thing, it is a reaction. Burning, also called combustion, happens when a fuel mixes with oxygen in air and gets hot enough to react. That reaction makes more heat and light, which keeps it going.

guess.question: To keep a fire going, what do you need?
guess.why: Fire is a reaction between fuel and oxygen, and it needs heat to keep it started. Take away any one and it stops.

steps.title: Heat changes stuff
steps.text: Second truth: matter changes form when heated. Solid wax can melt into liquid wax. If it gets even hotter, that liquid can turn into vapor — an invisible gas. Jargon check: vapor just means the gas form of something that is usually liquid or solid.

guess.question: What happens to wax when you heat it?
guess.why: Heat first melts solid wax to liquid, then hot liquid turns to vapor, an invisible gas that can mix with air and burn.

steps.title: The wick is a pump
steps.text: The wick is a straw, not a log. It is twisted cotton with tiny spaces between fibers. Melted wax climbs up those spaces by capillary action — the same pull that makes water climb a paper towel. The flame's heat melts the wax right around the wick, so there is always liquid to climb.

guess.question: The wick is made of twisted cotton threads with tiny gaps. What will it do in melted wax?
options: it melts the wax far away
it soaks up liquid wax like a straw
guess.why: Tiny gaps pull liquid up by capillary action, the same way a paper towel soaks up spilled water.

steps.title: The invisible gas burns
steps.text: At the hot top of the wick, liquid wax boils into vapor. That invisible wax gas mixes with oxygen in the air and reacts — that is the bright flame you see. The wick's tip gets hot enough to glow and slowly turn to ash, but it is too thin to keep a big flame going by itself.

guess.question: Look closely: the bright flame floats just above the wick, with a dark gap in between. What is burning up there?
guess.why: Hot liquid wax at the wick turns to vapor. Only gas mixed with air can burn with a clean flame, which is why the flame hovers where vapor meets air.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: heat melts wax, the wick pulls liquid wax up, liquid turns to vapor, vapor + oxygen + heat burns into light and heat. That heat melts more wax. The wax is the fuel that runs out. The wick just keeps the cycle in one small, steady spot.

guess.question: After an hour, the candle is shorter and lighter. Which part was used up as fuel?
options: the wax, because the candle loses weight
the wick, because the flame touches it
guess.why: The missing weight is mostly wax that turned to vapor and burned into hot gases. The wick is still almost the same length.

steps.title: Relight the smoke
steps.text: Safe test with an adult: blow out a candle, then quickly hold a lit match 2 cm above the wick in the thin white smoke. The flame will jump down to the wick without touching it. That smoke is unburned wax vapor — and you just proved vapor burns.

steps.title: Smother it
steps.text: Use your model: no oxygen, no combustion. Trapped air soon has too little oxygen to react with wax vapor. The flame shrinks, makes less heat, melts less wax, makes less vapor, and goes out — even though wick and wax are still there.

guess.question: You cover a burning candle with a clear glass jar. It burns a bit, then dies. Why?
options: it runs out of wax vapor and gets smothered
guess.why: The flame uses up the oxygen in the jar and makes gases that block fresh air. Without oxygen, wax vapor cannot react, so heat drops and the cycle stops.

steps.title: Faraday's candle talks
steps.text: In the 1860s, scientist Michael Faraday gave famous talks for kids using just a candle. He showed wax traveling up the wick, burning as vapor, and turning into water and invisible gases. He called a candle a little chemical factory, and his book is still free to read today.

steps.title: Why two colors?
steps.text: Next time, notice: why is the bottom of the flame blue and the top yellow-orange? Hint: blue is where vapor and fresh oxygen mix perfectly and burn clean; yellow is where tiny hot carbon bits glow before they finish burning.

claims.text: Candle wax is fuel made mostly of hydrocarbons that can melt and then vaporize when heated.
Combustion is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases heat and light.
The wick draws liquid wax upward by capillary action and holds the flame in place.
In a burning candle it is mainly wax vapor, not the solid wax or the wick itself, that burns in the flame.
The wick slowly chars and is consumed, but much more slowly than the wax, so wax is the main fuel that runs out.
Michael Faraday explained the chemistry of the candle in his 1860s lectures The Chemical History of a Candle.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg - Faraday Chemical History of a Candle

output.title: Why ice floats in your drink
output.summary: Ice takes up more space than the same water as a liquid, so it is lighter for its size and floats.
learningObjectives: Explain that ice is lighter for its size than water, so it floats.
Use heavy-for-size to predict float or sink.
misconceptionNotes: Hard or cold does not mean heavy. Ice feels hard but it is still lighter for its size than water, so it floats.

concepts.label: dense means heavy for its size

steps.title: Cubes that bob up
steps.text: You drop ice cubes in your drink with a plink! They bob back up and sit near the top. Part is under the drink, part sticks out in the air. Hard rocks sink, so why does hard ice float?

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: Ice floats because it is lighter for its size than your drink. Frozen water takes up more room, so it bobs up to the top.

steps.title: Tiny water pieces
steps.text: Everything around you is made of tiny pieces. Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules. They are too small to see, and they always wiggle and move.

guess.question: What is a molecule like in water?
options: tiny building blocks you cannot see
tiny ice cubes you can see
guess.why: Water is made of super tiny pieces that are too small to see.

steps.title: Heavy-for-size wins
steps.text: To float or sink, what matters is heavy-for-size. A big light leaf floats. A small heavy rock sinks. Scientists say dense for heavy-for-size.

guess.question: A rock and a leaf fall in a pond. Which sinks?
guess.why: Heavy-for-size things sink. Light-for-size things float.

steps.title: Freezing makes room
steps.text: In your freezer, water gets cold. The molecules slow down and hold on to each other. They make a spread-out shape, like building a tower with lots of empty space in it.

guess.question: When water freezes, what do the molecules do?
options: they make a spread-out tower with empty space
guess.why: Ice molecules hold arms out and make room with air-like empty space inside.

steps.title: Ice is light for its size
steps.text: So the same water takes up MORE room as ice. That means one ice cube is lighter than the same size sip of water. Ice is less heavy-for-size than water.

guess.question: An ice cube and the same size cup of water: which is lighter?
options: a cup of water with the same size
guess.why: The ice has empty space inside its shape, so it is lighter for its size.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Water cannot hold up something heavier-for-size than itself, so that sinks. But water CAN hold up ice, because ice is lighter-for-size. So up it bobs! That is why ice floats in your drink.

steps.title: Push and pop
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: put an ice cube in water and watch. Push it down gently with a spoon, then let go. Does it pop back up? Watch where the top of the ice sits.

steps.title: What if ice was heavy?
steps.text: Water is special. Most liquids do the opposite. Think: if ice were heavier-for-size than water, just like a rock is to water, what would happen in your cup?

guess.question: Most things shrink and get heavier-for-size when frozen. If water acted like that, what would ice do?
options: it would sink to the bottom
it would still float on top
guess.why: If ice were heavier-for-size, water could not hold it up.

steps.title: The floating discovery
steps.text: Long, long ago, a thinker named Archimedes wondered about floating. He saw that water pushes up on things in it. People still use his idea today to tell what will float.

steps.title: From cubes to icebergs
steps.text: Look at your cube as it melts. It gets smaller but keeps floating. In oceans, huge floating ice mountains called icebergs do the same thing, with just a little tip showing above the sea.

claims.text: Water is made of tiny pieces called molecules that move around.
When water freezes, its molecules lock into a spread-out pattern, so ice takes up more space than the same amount of liquid water.
Because it takes up more space for the same amount of water, ice is lighter for its size than liquid water, which scientists call less dense.
Objects that are lighter for their size than the liquid they are in float, while heavier-for-size objects sink.
Ice floats in liquid water with part sticking up above the top.
The idea that floating is about pushing water out of the way goes back to Archimedes, who studied buoyancy in ancient Greece.

sources.title: USGS Water Science School: Water Density

problems.question: What is a molecule like in water?
Most things shrink and get heavier-for-size when frozen. If water acted like that, what would ice do?

output.title: What is in this glass?
output.summary: The glass holds water: zillions of tiny H2O molecules that slide past each other, plus unseen air and minerals if it is tap water.
learningObjectives: Say that water is made of tiny H2O molecules.
Explain that liquid water flows because molecules slide past each other.
misconceptionNotes: The glass does not hold nothing or just wetness. It holds matter made of tiny water molecules, plus tiny unseen air and minerals in tap water.

steps.title: A glass of see-through stuff
steps.text: You see a clear glass. Inside is a clear liquid. It has no color. You can see right through it. It looks plain. But what IS that clear stuff? Why is it wet and splashy and not hard like ice?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: In the glass is water. Water is made of super tiny pieces called molecules. Each water molecule is called H2O.

steps.title: Everything is made of tiny pieces
steps.text: First big truth: everything is made of super tiny pieces. They are too small to see. They are always moving a little. We call these tiny pieces molecules. Molecules are made of even tinier pieces called atoms.

guess.question: If we had super eyes, what would we see inside everything?
options: Lots of super tiny moving pieces
guess.why: All matter is made of tiny moving pieces, so water is too.

steps.title: The recipe for water
steps.text: Second big truth: a water molecule has its own recipe. H means hydrogen. O means oxygen. H2O means 2 hydrogen atoms stuck to 1 oxygen atom. Like Mickey Mouse ears: big head is oxygen, two small ears are hydrogen.

guess.question: What parts make one H2O water molecule?
guess.why: H2O means 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom joined together.

steps.title: Slide and hug
steps.text: In the glass, zillions of H2O molecules crowd together. They hug a little. But they can slide past each other. That is why water pours, splashes, and takes the shape of the glass.

guess.question: Why can water pour and splash?
guess.why: Water molecules hold on a little but can slide, so water flows.

steps.title: Tiny visitors
steps.text: If this is tap water, it is not only H2O. It also has tiny visitors: air bubbles too small to see, and minerals from rocks and soil. They are safe in tiny amounts. They can give water its taste.

guess.question: Tap water is mostly H2O, plus what else?
options: Tiny air and mineral bits you cannot see
guess.why: Tap water picks up tiny bits of air and minerals on its way to you.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the glass holds water. That means zillions of H2O molecules sliding around. Plus, if from the tap, super tiny bits of air and minerals hiding inside.

steps.title: Pour it, freeze it
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: pour a little water from one cup to another. Watch it flow. Now put one cup in the freezer for hours. It gets hard. Same H2O! Cold just makes the molecules stop sliding and lock in place as ice.

steps.title: Is steam still water?
steps.text: Think: hot steam from soup looks like a cloud. Is it still water? Yes! Hot H2O molecules move super fast and fly apart into air. We call that steam. Cooled down, they become liquid water again.

guess.question: A pot boils and steam rises. What is the steam?
options: It turned into different stuff that is not water
It is still H2O, just moving faster and spreading out
guess.why: Heating makes H2O molecules move fast and fly apart as gas, but they are still H2O.

steps.title: Who found the recipe?
steps.text: Long ago people thought water was just water. About 250 years ago, two men, Henry Cavendish and Antoine Lavoisier, did tests. They made water from two gases: hydrogen and oxygen. That showed water has a recipe: H2O.

steps.title: Where did your water travel?
steps.text: Next time you drink, remember: you are drinking zillions of tiny H2O Mickeys. Ask a grown-up: where does our water come from? A river? A lake? Under the ground? All water on Earth gets used again and again.

claims.text: Water is a clear, colorless liquid with no taste or smell at room temperature.
A water molecule is a tiny piece of water made of two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom, written H2O.
All matter is made of very tiny moving pieces called atoms and molecules.
Liquid water flows because its molecules can move and slide past each other while still sticking together a little.
Drinking water from a tap also has very tiny bits of air and minerals mixed in that you cannot see.
In the 1780s Henry Cavendish and Antoine Lavoisier showed water is not a single simple substance but is made from hydrogen and oxygen.

sources.title: USGS Water Science School - What is water?

output.title: Why are salt grains little cubes?
output.summary: Salt is alternating sodium and chloride ions. They stack so each ion has 6 opposite neighbors, forming a cubic 3D checkerboard, so grains grow and break as tiny cubes.
learningObjectives: Explain that salt is a stack of alternating charged ions, not molecules.
Explain how a cubic stack makes cubic grains.
misconceptionNotes: Salt cubes are not cut or molded into cubes by machines — the cube shape grows on its own from how the ions stack.
A salt grain is not one NaCl molecule — it contains trillions of ions in a repeating pattern.

concepts.label: ion - an atom with electric charge
ionic bond - attraction between opposite charges

steps.title: Tiny boxes, not random crumbs
steps.text: Look close at table salt with a magnifier. Many grains are tiny, clear boxes with flat sides and square corners. Ground pepper makes random jagged bits, but salt keeps making little cubes. Why would shapeless salty water dry into neat cubes?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Salt grains are little cubes because salt is built from tiny charged balls that stack in an alternating 3D checkerboard. That stack is a cube pattern, so even a tiny piece looks like a cube.

steps.title: Salt is + and - balls that attract
steps.text: First truth you can trust: salt is not one thing. It is two kinds of ions. An ion is an atom with an electric charge. Salt has positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions. Second truth: opposite charges attract. So the ions pull on each other strongly.

guess.question: Sodium is + and chloride is -. What will they do?
guess.why: Opposite charges attract, so they pull together. That attraction is what holds salt solid.

steps.title: Nature seeks the cozy arrangement
steps.text: Systems settle where energy is lowest, like a ball rolling downhill. For charges, lowest energy means each + wants - neighbors, not + neighbors. So they will alternate: + - + - and never clump + with + if they can avoid it.

guess.question: If you could arrange + and - balls to be most stable, how would you do it?
options: Same charges together to save space
Opposite charges next to each other to lower energy
guess.why: Putting + next to - gives the strongest pull and lowest energy. Nature settles to the lowest energy.

steps.title: Six neighbors each
steps.text: In a line, each ion can have 2 opposite neighbors. On a flat sheet, 4. In 3D salt, each sodium sits in the middle with 6 chlorides around it: up, down, front, back, left, right. And each chloride has 6 sodiums around it the same way.

guess.question: In 3D, how many opposite neighbors can one ball touch if you pack neatly?
options: 6 — up, down, left, right, front, back
guess.why: In 3D there are 6 directions at right angles. Salt uses all 6, so each sodium touches 6 chlorides.

steps.title: A 3D checkerboard
steps.text: Now repeat that pattern thousands of times in all three directions. You get a 3D checkerboard where + and - always alternate. Because the three directions are at right angles, the grid lines form squares and boxes, not diamonds or pyramids.

guess.question: If you repeat that up-down, left-right, front-back pattern over and over, what shape do you get?
guess.why: The three directions are at right angles, like the corner of a box. Repeating that builds cubes.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: the building block is a cube-shaped pattern of alternating ions. When the crystal grows, it adds more layers to flat faces. When it breaks, it splits between layers along flat faces. So the grain stays a cube, just bigger or smaller. No mold needed — the cube is the pattern itself.

steps.title: Grow your own cubes
steps.text: Test it safely: stir 3 spoonfuls of salt into half a cup of very warm water until no more dissolves. Pour into a shallow bowl and leave it still for 2-3 days. Look with a magnifier as water leaves. Ask an adult for help with hot water. Do you see new tiny squares and stair-step cubes growing?

steps.title: What about sugar?
steps.text: Use your rule: shape comes from stacking. If the pieces and stacking change, the outer shape should change. Check sugar crystals with a magnifier. They look like slanted bars and wedges, not cubes. That fits — different pieces, different stack, different shape.

guess.question: Sugar is made of big lopsided sugar molecules, not + and - balls. Will its crystals be perfect cubes like salt?
options: No, a different stacking should make a different shape
Yes, all crystals must be cubes
guess.why: Shape comes from the building block and stacking. Different blocks make different shapes — sugar makes slanted prisms, not cubes.

steps.title: Seeing inside with X-rays
steps.text: For a long time no one could see inside salt. In 1912 Max von Laue showed X-rays could bounce off crystals. In 1913 father and son William and Lawrence Bragg aimed X-rays at salt and read the pattern. It proved salt was a regular cubic lattice of alternating atoms — the checkerboard was real.

steps.title: Why does salt shatter?
steps.text: Next puzzle: salt shatters easily if you crush it, but a metal spoon bends. Both have repeating lattices. What is different about charged + and - layers sliding past each other versus neutral metal atoms? That difference explains why salt is brittle.

claims.text: Table salt is sodium chloride, made of positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions in a 1 to 1 ratio.
Opposite electric charges attract, so sodium and chloride ions pull toward each other to form ionic bonds.
In solid salt, the ions form a repeating 3D grid called a cubic crystal lattice where sodium and chloride alternate like squares on a 3D checkerboard.
In this lattice each ion is surrounded by 6 ions of the opposite charge — up, down, front, back, left, and right.
Because the pattern repeats equally in three directions at right angles, the natural shape and cleavage of the crystal is a cube.
A salt grain you see is usually one tiny single crystal or a clump of crystals, not a single molecule of NaCl.
claims.uncertainty: Size varies with grinding; table salt is often crushed cubes, while undisturbed slow growth makes clearer cubes.

claims.text: Other crystals with different building blocks and stacking make different shapes; for example table sugar forms non-cubic crystals.
Early work with X-rays in 1912-1913 by Max von Laue, William Bragg and Lawrence Bragg first proved salt has a regular cubic inner lattice.

output.title: Why does a cut apple turn brown?
output.summary: Air touches a cut apple, and enzymes help oxygen change apple juice into brown color.
learningObjectives: Tell that brown on a cut apple is a change made by air, not dirt.
Tell that oxygen plus apple juices plus enzymes make brown color.
Guess ways to slow browning by keeping air away.
misconceptionNotes: The brown is not dirt and not right away bad to eat; it is new brown chemicals made when air touches apple juice. We correct this kindly in the lesson.

steps.title: A white apple turns brown
steps.text: You cut an apple. It is white and juicy inside. Wait a little. The cut part turns brown. A whole apple does not do this. What makes the cut part change color? Is it dirt?

steps.title: Short answer
steps.text: Air touches the juicy cut. Air helps change the juice into brown color. It is not dirt.

steps.title: Air is there even if we do not see it
steps.text: First truth: air is all around us, even when we cannot see it. One part of air is called oxygen. We breathe it in.

guess.question: We are wrapped in what?
guess.why: Air is all around us, and it has a part called oxygen.

steps.title: Apples have juices and helpers inside
steps.text: Second truth: living things have tiny helpers called enzymes. An enzyme helps things change fast. An apple has juices and enzymes inside, kept safe by the skin.

guess.question: What is an enzyme?
options: tiny helpers that speed up changes
guess.why: Enzymes are helpers in living things that make some changes happen fast.

steps.title: Cutting opens the coat
steps.text: A whole apple has skin like a coat. Air cannot touch the juice inside. When you cut it, the coat is open. Air can now touch the wet cut.

guess.question: Which apple lets air touch the juice?
guess.why: The cut has no skin cover, so air can touch the wet inside.

steps.title: Helpers build brown bits
steps.text: At the cut, the helpers meet air and juice together. They help oxygen from air hold hands with the apple juice. This makes new tiny bits that look brown.

guess.question: What do the apple enzymes do at the cut?
options: they help oxygen and juice join
guess.why: They help oxygen from air join with apple juice to make brown color.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: cut opens the juice to air. Enzymes help oxygen change the juice into brown bits. Lots of brown bits add up. The cut looks brown.

guess.question: Why does the whole cut turn brown after a while?
guess.why: Many tiny brown bits add up until we see brown.

steps.title: Test it with three pieces
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up. Cut an apple into 3 pieces. Leave one open. Wrap one tight in clear wrap. Squeeze lemon juice on one. Wait 20 minutes. Which stays whitest? You kept air away or slowed the helpers.

steps.title: What about a pear?
steps.text: Think: you cut a pear. You leave it in air. Will it stay white? Use what you learned about air and helpers to guess, then look.

guess.question: What else should turn brown like this?
options: a cut pear or banana left in air
guess.why: Pears and bananas have similar juices and helpers, so air browns them too.

steps.title: How we found the helpers
steps.text: Long ago, people saw cut fruit turn brown. In the 1800s, scientists found the helpers called enzymes. They learned enzymes speed up changes in plants and in us.

steps.title: Keep it white
steps.text: Next, ask: how do stores keep apple slices white? Hint: no air packs and cool air slow the helpers. What would you invent for your lunchbox?

claims.text: A cut apple turns brown in minutes when left in air; this is called enzymatic browning.
Air contains oxygen gas that can join with other chemicals in a change called oxidation.
Apples contain natural chemicals called phenols and helper proteins called enzymes, especially polyphenol oxidase.
When cut, enzymes help oxygen join to apple chemicals to make new brown chemicals called melanins.
Apple skin keeps air away from the inside, so a whole apple does not turn brown inside.
Keeping air away or adding acid like lemon juice slows browning.
In the 1800s scientists learned that enzymes are helpers in living things that speed up chemical changes.
claims.uncertainty: Exact early dates vary by source, but 1800s work on enzymes is well described.

output.title: Why soap bubbles look rainbow
output.summary: A bubble is rainbow because light bounces off both sides of its thin skin and adds or cancels to pick colours.
learningObjectives: Tell that a bubble skin has two sides that both bounce light.
Tell that colours come from light waves adding and cancelling, not from dye.
Tell that skin thickness picks the colour we see.
misconceptionNotes: The soap does not dye the bubble rainbow — clear soapy water can still look rainbow because of bouncing light.

steps.title: A clear ball with rainbows
steps.text: You blow a clear bubble. It floats. Then — pink! Green! Blue! Swirls move on it like paint. The soap was clear. So where do the colours come from?

steps.title: Quick answer
steps.text: Light bounces off the front and back of the bubble skin. The two bounces mix. That mix keeps some colours and hides others, so you see rainbows.

steps.title: Light is waves, white is a mix
steps.text: First truth: light is like tiny waves. Wave means up-and-down while it moves. Second truth: white light is a mix. Red waves are long. Blue waves are short. Mixed, they look white.

guess.question: White daylight is really what?
guess.why: White light is red, orange, yellow, green, blue and more all mixed. We will need that to explain rainbows.

steps.title: Waves can add or cancel
steps.text: Third truth: waves can add or cancel. Up plus up makes big. Up plus down makes flat. Bright means added. Dark means cancelled.

guess.question: What happens when two same-size waves meet?
options: they just pass by each other
they can add up big or cancel to flat
guess.why: Up plus up makes a bigger wave. Up plus down can flatten out. This adding and cancelling is called interference.

steps.title: A bubble skin has two sides
steps.text: A bubble is not one thin wall. It is a thin skin of water. It has a front side and a back side. Light bounces off both. So two sets of light waves head to your eye.

guess.question: A bubble skin is super thin with two sides. How many bounces of light do we get?
options: two bounces, one from the front and one from the back
guess.why: Some light bounces off the front. Some goes in and bounces off the back. So your eye gets two sets of waves.

steps.title: Two bounces pick colours
steps.text: The two bounces travel a little bit more or less. For red, up may meet up and get bright. For green, up may meet down and go away. So one colour shines, one hides.

guess.question: Red and green waves both bounce twice. Can one cancel while the other adds up?
options: it depends on the skin thickness, red may cancel and green may add
guess.why: Yes. Red waves are longer than green waves, so the same thickness adds one up but flattens the other. That is how colours are picked.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text: Put it together: different thickness makes different colours. Thicker spots pick one colour. Thinner spots pick another. Water slides down, so the top gets thin and colours swirl and change.

guess.question: If the skin is thicker at the bottom and thinner at the top, will colours be different?
options: yes, thick spots and thin spots show different colours
no, the whole bubble must be one colour
guess.why: Thickness picks the winner colour. Different thickness in each spot means a swirly rainbow map.

steps.title: Watch a bubble fade
steps.text: Try this with a grown-up: blow a big bubble and do not touch it. Just watch. Do colours slide down? Does the top get dark just before it pops? That dark spot is the thinnest skin where most light cancels.

steps.title: What about oil rainbows?
steps.text: Think: an oil puddle also shines rainbow, with no soap at all. Does our idea still work? Yes! Oil makes a thin skin too.

guess.question: You see rainbow swirls on a car-park oil puddle. No soap there. What do you expect?
options: rainbow swirls from thin bouncing skin
guess.why: Oil also makes a super-thin skin on water. Light bounces twice there too and picks colours. No dye needed.

steps.title: People who looked closely
steps.text: Long ago, Robert Hooke and Isaac Newton looked closely at thin colours like these. They saw rings and rainbows in thin glass and bubbles. Their careful looking helped us learn about light waves later.

steps.title: Shine with no paint
steps.text: Look around: peacock feathers, beetles, CDs, and soap all shine without paint. Next time, ask: where is the thin skin that bounces light twice?

claims.text: A soap bubble is a very thin skin of soapy water around air, with an outside surface and an inside surface.
Light bounces, or reflects, off the outside and inside surfaces of a thin soap skin.
Light moves like a tiny wave, and two waves can add together to get brighter or cancel to get darker.
White daylight is made of many colours mixed together, and each colour has a different wave size.
In a thin skin, the thickness decides which colour gets brighter and which colour cancels out, so we see different colours in different spots.
The soapy water slowly runs down, so the top of a bubble gets thinner and its colours move and change.
The same bouncing-light trick makes rainbow colours on oil puddles and on some bird feathers and insect wings.
Early scientists like Robert Hooke and Isaac Newton studied these colours in thin skins and plates in the 1600s-1700s and helped explain them as light waves bouncing.
claims.uncertainty: Exact dates and full wave explanation came later, but Hooke and Newton made key early observations of thin-plate colours.

output.title: Why thin strings sing high
output.summary: Thinner strings are lighter per inch, so the same tension accelerates them faster and they vibrate more times per second — and we hear faster vibration as higher pitch.
learningObjectives: Link pitch to how fast a string vibrates.
Explain that lighter strings speed up and reverse faster under the same tension.
Use length, tension, and thickness to predict pitch change.
